headline: This law updates federal rules for private commercial rocket launches, extends some liability protections, and sets up rights for U.S. citizens to recover space resources.
what_it_does: It changes how the Department of Transportation handles licenses and experimental permits for commercial rockets and reentry vehicles, including reusable suborbital vehicles. It extends certain liability insurance and claim-waiver rules for space flight participants through FY2025 and gives federal courts exclusive jurisdiction over certain third-party claims from licensed launches. It also directs agencies to study space traffic management, space situational awareness data, and a possible future safety framework, and it creates a framework for U.S. citizens to commercially explore and recover space resources.

who_it_affects.group: Commercial space launch and reentry companies
who_it_affects.how: They face changed licensing and experimental permit rules, liability insurance and financial responsibility requirements, and possible future safety standards.
Their liability insurance coverage and reciprocal waiver of claims rules are extended through FY2025.

who_it_affects.group: Government astronauts, including NASA designees and international partner astronauts
who_it_affects.how: Certain commercial space launch requirements now apply to them when they are carried on a launch or reentry vehicle.

who_it_affects.group: U.S. citizens pursuing space resource recovery
who_it_affects.how: They are entitled to possess, own, transport, use, and sell asteroid or space resources they lawfully recover, subject to federal authorization and supervision.
Congress expresses that they should protect themselves from potential liability and compensate third parties, and GAO must report on including their property in federal indemnification.

who_it_affects.group: Operators of the International Space Station
who_it_affects.how: NASA must keep the ISS viable and available for U.S. use through at least FY2024.

when_it_takes_effect: Enacted November 25, 2015; several provisions run through FY2025 or FY2024, and many reporting and study deadlines apply afterward.
